subject: operating-systems
title: Scheduling algorithms
summary: CPU scheduling algorithms choose which runnable process or thread receives a processor next.

questions.prompt: Which policy selects the runnable job with the smallest estimated CPU burst?
questions.answerKey: Shortest-job-first (SJF) chooses the shortest estimated next CPU burst.
questions.explanation: FCFS uses arrival order and round robin uses time slices.

questions.prompt: What is the defining mechanism of round-robin scheduling?
options: A fixed time quantum and rotation among ready tasks
Running the oldest task to completion
Always selecting the largest memory process
questions.answerKey: Round robin gives each runnable task a time quantum before rotating.
questions.explanation: A timer interrupt enables preemption at the quantum boundary.

questions.prompt: A round-robin quantum is made extremely large. Which behavior does it approach?
questions.answerKey: With a very large quantum, tasks usually finish before rotation, resembling FCFS.
questions.explanation: The exact behavior also depends on arrivals and blocking.

questions.prompt: Why can strict priority scheduling starve low-priority work?
options: Low-priority tasks are never placed in memory
A continuous stream of higher-priority tasks can always preempt it
Priority queues cannot contain more than one task
The CPU cannot execute low-priority instructions
questions.answerKey: Without aging or another fairness mechanism, high-priority arrivals can postpone low-priority tasks indefinitely.
questions.explanation: Starvation is a fairness problem, not an inability to execute the code.

questions.prompt: For jobs A=0/5 ms and B=1/2 ms under non-preemptive FCFS, calculate each waiting time.
questions.answerKey: A starts at 0 and waits 0 ms. B starts when A finishes at 5 ms, so B waits 5 - 1 = 4 ms.
questions.explanation: Waiting time is start time minus arrival time.

questions.prompt: Choose a scheduling policy for an interactive terminal and justify two design concerns.
questions.answerKey: A preemptive policy such as round robin, often combined with priorities, is appropriate. A bounded quantum improves response time, while fairness/aging prevents background work from starving; context-switch overhead must also be controlled.
questions.explanation: There is no single universally best policy; the justification must match interactive goals.
